title: Black holes and gravitational waves. Padua pushes calculations beyond the limits of precision
content:
Black holes are celestial objects, compact bodies that in some respects are still mysterious; for this reason, research work is continuing in order to understand fully how they function, addressing the theories of relativity and quantum physics.

Among these lines of research, one major challenge in contemporary physics is the ever more precise calculation of how two black holes attract one another. These calculations, in fact, determine the interpretation of gravitational waves and the possibility of reconstructing the cosmic events that generated them.

An international collaboration in which the Department of Physics and Astronomy “Galileo Galilei” of the University of Padua, together with the Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), plays a central role has now added a new piece to this research path. The results are described in two scientific papers published in the journal Physical Review Letters, one of the most prestigious in the field of physics: the first on 9 September 2026, "Six-Loop Gravitational Interactions at the Sixth Post-Newtonian Order", the second on 12 November 2026, "All-order structure of static gravitational interactions and the seventh post-Newtonian potential".

The studies bring the calculation of the static component of the gravitational interaction between two compact bodies (black holes) to the sixth and seventh degree of post-Newtonian approximation: that is, increasingly advanced levels of the corrections through which Einstein’s general relativity extends Newton’s description of gravity.

More specifically, the first paper tackles six-loop calculations, mathematical structures represented through Feynman diagrams, providing the most technically demanding piece needed to complete the conservative dynamics at the sixth level. The second introduces a general formula for deriving the static contributions at odd levels, starting from the results of the lower levels, and applies it to the seventh level.

The scientific advances presented in the two publications essentially amount to progress in calculation and a new understanding of the mathematical structure of gravitational interaction. These results have been made possible by the meeting of ideas and the continuous refinement of calculation techniques, important steps towards an ever more detailed reading of the universe through gravitational waves.

When two black holes orbit one another, they emit gravitational waves and gradually draw closer until they merge. To obtain information from the observed signals, researchers compare them with theoretical predictions: the more accurate these are, the better it is possible to determine the properties of the sources and put Einstein’s theory to the test.

«Our work builds a bridge between the physics of the infinitely small and that of large astrophysical objects. We use and develop methods conceived to study elementary particles in order to tackle a problem in general relativity: calculating with ever greater precision the
way in which two black holes interact,» explains Pierpaolo Mastrolia, Professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy "Galileo Galilei" of the University of Padua, as well as an associated researcher at INFN.
«These works are the result of a long-term scientific investment. The continuity of research in Padua, the training of young researchers and the exchange of expertise with colleagues at AEI were crucial in achieving this milestone,» Mastrolia further emphasises.

Future observatories, including Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer and the LISA space mission, make the development of precise models even more urgent. The two papers provide new ingredients for describing the phase in which compact bodies draw closer together, while the construction of complete waveforms will require further new developments.
